 How iFood&#8217;s generative AI connects personalization and communication through rigorous engineering patterns to scale unique user experiences Início Cultura e Carreiras Dados & IA Engenharia Produto & Design Sobre o iFood pt-BR Início Cultura e Carreiras Dados & IA Engenharia Produto & Design Sobre o iFood pt-BR Home Artigo Dados & IA 02 mar. How iFood’s generative AI connects personalization and communication through rigorous engineering patterns to scale unique user experiences Leitura de 11 minutos How iFood’s generative AI connects personalization and communication through rigorous engineering patterns to scale unique user experiences From Grouped Campaigns to Individual Decisions [4:30 PM, Tuesday] Haven’t had lunch yet, right? The Mushroom Risotto you love is waiting for you 🍄 This is not a generic discount, nor a message sent to millions of people simultaneously. It is a notification that seems to know your routine and, including that lunch delay that has become a Tuesday habit. Instead of interrupting, it arrives at the right time. Instead of pushing an offer, it makes sense. It seems written for you. When communication sounds like this, it ceases to be noise and begins to feel like a real conversation. And this is the type of communication that iFood is building. The traditional push communication model was built to scale volume, not relevance. Push is cheap and the business impact is immediate. The more messages we send, the less attention we receive. The less attention we receive, the more we try to compensate with volume. And thus we enter a vicious cycle where the quantity of pushes grows and content quality plummets. The Real Problem: From Segments to Individuals For a long time, push notifications were treated as just another CRM (Customer Relationship Management) channel: take a segment, write a friendly standard text, choose a reasonable time and send. It works… to a certain point. In the end, segmentations compress different people into the same group and the result is a message that is okay for a few and irrelevant for many. Illustration of generic notification for large audience. What hyper-personalization does is change the decision unit. Instead of trying to find the best push for a group, you try to make the best decision for an individual. And this seems like a technical detail, but it is a product change: two people in the same segment can have different routines, different tastes, and different tolerances to interruptions. This is why, when it goes wrong, it is not just “low performance”; it is noise. Noise becomes ignoring. Ignoring becomes opt-out. The interesting part is that this problem did not exist due to lack of intention. It was always difficult to do “real” hyper-personalization because it requires three things simultaneously: rich behavioral signals , a reliable feedback loop , and the ability to make millions of micro-decisions daily without becoming operational chaos. For a long time, the solution was segmentation + rules + templates. It was what worked. But it was fragile: too generic to seem useful, too specific to scale manually. And then comes the turning point. Technology here is not the starting point; it is what enables this experience. Today, it is possible to combine billions of daily and granular data from the application, recommendation systems and models (including Large Language Models (LLM)) and transform push notifications into a small decision engine: choose the subject, choose the moment and reduce friction. Everything at the individual level, without depending on crude groupings. Three Critical Decisions: The New Product Architecture In practice, this becomes three decisions that simultaneously compose a new product: What to say? When we started building this product, it became clear that it did not make sense to “invent content” from scratch. We already had within the company one of the best possible sources: iFood’s curated recommendations. They become a menu of possibilities for the model to work with: interesting options, with high quality, and at the same time specific to the user. The LLM enters to choose well, capture semantics in user complexity and explain in a natural, short, human way, without looking like a template. When to speak? The right time is not a universal time, nor a “segment” time. It is personal. Some people repeat patterns by day of the week, some people alternate categories by time of day, some people only engage when they have already browsed the app. Understanding behavior here means looking at trends and routines: typical consumption times by category, weekly repetitions, variations by context, recent iterations within the app or even where you are. Sending ceases to be just a dispatch and becomes a perfect fit. How to reduce the journey? Even when the message is perfect, much dies in friction. If the user opens the push and lands on a generic screen, they have to search, compare, choose again, and this reintroduces bias and the chance of giving up. Therefore deep link is not a detail: it is part of hyper-personalization. Opening the app directly on the item and seeing a delicious and interesting image of the item you just received in the push, with a clear “add to cart” button, transforms interest into action with one click. When these three things work together, for example, the right subject, right time and short path, the coolest part happens: they generate “organic” orders. Not because a “higher” message was inserted, or because a discount was added. But because, at that moment, for that person, that was interesting. And when push becomes utility, it stops seeming like marketing trying to push something and starts sounding like a good suggestion. This is when notification becomes something natural and welcome. “The ideal notification is almost invisible: it arrives when the person is receptive, talks about something they really consider and, when opened, resolves the journey with the minimum number of steps.” LLMs Beyond the Chatbot LLMs usually appear in chatbots, but here their role is different. Instead of answering questions, we use this type of model as part of a decision system. It helps identify patterns of taste, schedule and habits and transform these signals into short messages, sent when they make the most sense. The idea is that communication is relevant to those who receive it. Engagement and clicks come as a consequence. Source: qualitative research data with FoodLovers in 2025. Values presented as variation relative to traditional push baseline. POC (Proof of Concept) Preview Before thinking about scale, we started small: we did a POC with iFood employees and conducted qualitative research to understand if this new type of push really made a difference. The feedback was clear to take the next step. After validating the product, the cost of operating at iFood’s scale (processing billions of tokens every day) became the main engineering and sustainability challenge. Figure 1. Percentage of superior variation (increment) relative to reference CTR (Click-Through Rate) After that, we ran an experiment with about 10 thousand users to validate whether the increase in relevance also translated into business metrics. It worked. But the most difficult question remained: does this effect sustain over time? We expanded the test to 1 million users over a month. The result was consistent, with significant engagement increase throughout the period. The product value is clear, but how to make this viable from a cost perspective? We tested different models, smaller architectures and began investing in consecutive fine tunings of open source LLM models using success examples. We built a self-feeding flow: notifications that work better help train increasingly efficient models, capable of generating more relevant messages using fewer tokens and parameters. The Flow is illustrated in Figure 2. Figure 2. High-level flow of iFood’s hyper-personalized push notification creation Data sources include order history and curated recommendations, used to define push content, and the Large Commerce Model (LCM) Profile, which describes user habits, preferences and behaviors inferred from clicks, orders and interactions with iFood, being used to define the tone and semantic hooks of the message. This data feeds the LCM content generation model, responsible for generating the push and defining the best sending time. Before dispatch, notifications go through guardrails and blocklists, described in the section below, to avoid unwanted communications. Next, all pushes go through a business prioritization system, responsible for delivering notifications from all iFood verticals through business rules. Finally, the push is sent and success KPIs are collected, such as clicked pushes and pushes that resulted in orders. These KPIs feed back into the model fine-tuning process, closing the continuous improvement cycle. With these learnings, the project ceased to be just an experiment and began to define a new communication standard at iFood. Today, this system already operates in production for about 25 million users, resulting in billions of tokens being processed daily*, and the expectation is to gradually expand and improve this approach to even more scenarios and communication surfaces. With each new iteration, the model becomes more efficient, more precise and more aligned with each person’s context. Traditional pushes are gradually being replaced by a living system that continuously learns and makes individualized decisions about what to say and when to say it. *For more technical details on how we do daily inference of billions of tokens using open source models LLMs in Production: Security Without Human Review Using LLMs in such a critical stage of a company’s communication brings real risks. A wrong message is not just a technical bug. An error can break user trust and even generate legal implications. At iFood’s scale, reviewing notification by notification is simply not feasible. Nevertheless, understanding what the system is producing is essential. Instead of trying to control each push individually, we need mechanisms to observe system behavior as a whole, identify deviations and act quickly when something goes beyond expectations. One of the approaches we use for this is called LLM as a Judge : another LLM responsible for evaluating the outputs of the main model. We clearly defined what the message objective was and asked the Judge to evaluate whether it meets expected criteria. Today, our main metrics are linked to real risks of this type of system, such as toxicity and hallucination. This process runs continuously for a sample of the base and allows us to monitor quality and security at scale, without depending on manual review. Toxicity : Verifies presence of offensive, disrespectful languages, suggestions and attitudes that promote negativity and competitiveness Hallucination : Verifies if content mentions details that are not present in the data: invention of items, merchants and promotions, errors when citing items that do not exist in a merchant and errors in creating the message deeplink. Additionally, we combine this monitoring with more traditional guardrails: blocklists and programmatic validations. They prevent, for example, sending messages with potentially problematic terms, incorrect discount values, invented promotions or wrong references to items and merchants. Each LLM-based system requires its own metrics, aligned with its business context. The objective is not to completely eliminate risk, but to reduce the probability of harmful content and, mainly, detect them quickly when something goes beyond expectations. Orchestration at Scale: The Next Challenge of Hyper-Personalization The future of this strategy is not “personalizing more,” it is orchestrating better. When you are talking about something like 200 million pushes sent per day, the problem ceases to be delivery and becomes governance: who has priority, which message competes with which, and how to ensure the user does not become a battlefield between verticals. And this becomes even more real when everything grows simultaneously: food delivery, market, club, pharmacy and promotions (which, in practice, become a “vertical” transversal pressuring all others). In practice, each has legitimate reasons to speak: restaurant food is immediate and the company’s core, club has relationship logic and perceived value, promotions have urgency and short-term efficiency. But the user is one. Personalization without coordination becomes a paradox: each team is “right” locally, but the global result for the same person can be noise. The challenge becomes maintaining individualized message without losing business decisions, balancing simultaneous objectives, marketplace restrictions and priorities that change daily. And there is a point that few people face head on: finding the right moment to stay quiet . At scale, silence becomes a product feature. If the system only learns to speak when it has something to gain, it loses the most important side: preserving user attention for when it really matters. Knowing not to send, especially when several verticals “want” space, is as sophisticated a decision as choosing the perfect content. The Human Challenge: Mindset Change Finally, perhaps the biggest challenge is human: the mindset change. Marketing is accustomed to controlling campaigns, calendar and message; individualized decisions are, by definition, less “controllable” on the surface. This affects processes, approvals and trust in the system. For this evolution to work, it needs to be joint: product, engineering, architecture, data, marketing and business units aligned on the same question: “what is the best decision for this person, given today’s business priorities?” The idea that control ceases to be manual and becomes a set of decision criteria and guardrails: explicit priorities, frequency limits and clear rules for when verticals conflict. Compartilhe: Mateus Aguiar Data Scientist Mateus é mineiro e Cientista de Dados no iFood. Vive em Itacaré, na Bahia, entre códigos, ondas e café.
